name: Adam Walsh

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, AI companies or government. This is confidential, and I am not looking for a right answer. What fills a normal workday?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m 27, trained through a music master’s, and people hire me to play piano, arrange scores and teach. I’m trusted with difficult parts, but paid less than that sounds.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Where does the work feel good, and where does it grind?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like helping a singer settle into a phrase that finally fits. The grind is carrying three small invoices around in my head and wondering which one will clear before rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d still unlock the rehearsal room at eight, teach three piano pupils and play an evening set at the café. Between them I arrange scores and send invoices; the pay comes in small pieces. I’d tell the café owner that AI Plateau leaves the live set much as it was. A quicker booking message is fine if we still agree the fee ourselves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m already watching my bank account by the day. I have under a month saved, and there are few comparable music jobs near my flat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep the café set and my pupil timetable, then start logging every late invoice this Friday. If two clients pay together, I’d put twenty into savings rather than buy another pedal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m uneasy about the work, but anxious about the bills I already have. The word plateau does not flatten my electricity bill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much does a late fee change your week?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: One missing lesson payment sends groceries to Sunday, when the café pays me. I do not have enough saved to treat a late fee as nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ask family for help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My parents would feed me, and I am grateful for that. I would ask only if rent itself were at risk, because I want to keep working.

say: I’d say the **live café set** and piano lessons still need me in the room.
I would accept simpler **booking messages** while keeping the fee agreement between people.
think: I have less than a **month saved**, so late lesson payments still change my grocery plans.
Few nearby **music jobs** would replace the café or teaching if either stopped.
do: Keep the **café set** and three piano pupils on their current schedule.
Log **late invoices** each Friday and save twenty when two clients pay together.
feel: I feel **anxious** about ordinary bills, even if AI itself brings little change.
fieldNote: His concern begins with **irregular income**, not a claim that AI has already taken paid work.
The planned **twenty** goes to savings only when two clients pay, showing how narrow his margin is.
S0.quote: The word plateau does not flatten my electricity bill.

steps.text: Keep the café set and three piano lessons each week
Save twenty when two clients pay together

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The first sign might be a client asking for fewer arrangements rather than cancelling my piano set. I already use an AI tool sometimes to sort rough lesson notes, but I check every line. I’d tell clients Steady Disruption could make simple backing tracks cheaper, while a room of people still hears the difference in a live player. I would ask the café to confirm dates in writing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think the little arranging jobs that fill my Tuesday gaps could go. A passable backing track can steal a Tuesday fee before anyone touches my piano keys. My chord voicing is better, but clients may not pay for the difference.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I’d ask an older accompanist to show me how she checks AI scores for wrong notes. If arranging fees fall in the first year, I’d replace one empty Tuesday with two paid beginner lessons, if families enroll.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That makes me anxious, though I can still test the tools without handing over a whole performance. I would rather learn from someone who has made mistakes in public.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the two lessons earn?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two paid lessons could replace one small arrangement each week. That works only if both families keep booking their slots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why ask someone older about AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She understands how a real singer needs to breathe and has caught printed score errors for years. I trust her ear more than a tool demonstration.

say: I’d tell clients **simple backing tracks** may get cheaper while live players can still earn a room’s attention.
I’d ask the **café** to confirm dates in writing before I count the income.
think: My small **arranging fees** could fall first because a passable draft is cheap.
A client may not pay for **voicing skill** when the draft sounds good enough on a phone.
do: Ask an experienced **accompanist** this month to show me how she checks AI scores.
Add two Tuesday **beginner lessons** if families enroll after arranging fees fall.
feel: I feel **anxious**, with enough control to learn carefully and try a lesson change.
fieldNote: He uses AI **occasionally**, but seeks a musician’s judgment before trusting generated scores.
Two added lessons are **conditional** on both a fee loss and families enrolling; he does not assume demand.
S1.quote: A passable backing track can steal a Tuesday fee before anyone touches my piano keys.

steps.text: Ask experienced accompanist to demonstrate checking AI scores
Add two Tuesday beginner lessons if arranging fees fall and families enroll

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If AGI by 2028 handles almost every thinking task, my arranging work and lesson planning could be replaced quickly. Hands-on playing has until capable robots around 2031, but clients may buy generated sound before then. I’d tell the café owner I can still play the dates on the calendar, but we need to discuss fees honestly. I would not tell pupils that a master’s degree protects a booking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A machine that writes a convincing score in 2028 could wipe out one of my few weekday earners. My parents can put dinner on the table, but they cannot pay the rent on my flat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d price the smallest room at the community centre this month and ask parents whether four pupils want group practice. If arranging income vanishes in the first year after 2028, I’d cancel my paid rehearsal room and use that group space only if it covers hire.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed. I can adjust a lesson plan, but two years will not turn thin savings into a safety net.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your parents that first week?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say the arranging invoices stopped and ask my parents for meals. I would not ask them to promise rent money they do not have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you train for another career straightaway?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would first test the group and the cheaper room. Another degree costs money I do not have, and I need earnings sooner than a course would bring.

say: I’d keep the **café dates** already promised but discuss future fees honestly.
I would tell pupils a **music degree** does not guarantee paid bookings under fast AGI.
think: Arranging and lesson **planning** could go in 2028, before capable performance robots arrive around 2031.
Family **meals** could help, but my parents cannot cover the rent on my flat.
do: Price the small **community room** this month and ask four pupils about group practice.
Cancel the paid **rehearsal room** if arranging income vanishes after 2028, provided group fees cover hire.
feel: I feel **alarmed** because two years cannot turn my thin savings into a safety net.
fieldNote: He distinguishes lost **thinking work** in 2028 from the later robot threat to hands-on playing.
His plan relies on **four pupils** and room costs; family help is food, not rent or an easy escape.
S2.quote: My parents can put dinner on the table, but they cannot pay the rent on my flat.

steps.text: Price community room and ask four pupils about group practice
Cancel paid rehearsal room if arranging fees vanish and group covers hire

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years would let me see which clients actually stop buying arrangements by 2031. Robots able to perform like people would follow around 2034, so the live set has a longer clock. I’d tell my pupils I intend to teach through the change and show them how to hear a false note in generated music. I would not sell them a promise that live fees stay level.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The extra years matter because I can learn a proven tool and build a teaching list without borrowing for another degree. I still expect the arranging side to shrink by 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask the accompanist for one score-checking session this winter, then try the method on my own arrangements. If pupils ask for it, I’d offer a small listening class next summer only when fees cover the room. In the first year after 2031, I would repeat the class only while it pays for the room and my teaching time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m anxious, but five years gives me a sequence I can afford. I would rather test one class than buy equipment because someone says I must.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the listening class teach?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would play two versions of one phrase and ask pupils to mark the singer’s breath. A listening class might teach children where a singer needs air, even if a computer writes every note.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you stop arranging now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I need the arranging fees while they still exist. Those same scores could help me teach better listening, so I would not quit today.

say: I’d tell pupils **listening skill** matters even when a machine can draft a score.
I would warn clients that **arranging** could change by 2031 and live playing faces robots around 2034.
think: Five years lets me test a **teaching list** without borrowing for another qualification.
I still expect **arranging income** to shrink before live performance does.
do: Take one winter **score-checking session** with the accompanist and test it on my arrangements.
Offer a summer **listening class** if pupils ask and fees cover the room; repeat after 2031 only if it pays.
feel: I feel **anxious**, but the longer warning gives me an affordable order of steps.
fieldNote: He chooses a **proven method** learned from a colleague, matching his cautious approach to technology.
The new class needs both **pupil interest** and enough fees to cover the room; arranging continues meanwhile.
S3.quote: A listening class might teach children where a singer needs air, even if a computer writes every note.

steps.text: Learn score checking from accompanist in one winter session
Offer summer listening class if pupils ask and fees cover room

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In ten years I’d be 37, and the music business could change a lot before AGI arrives in 2036. The thinking parts would go then; robots capable of hands-on performance would be around 2039. I’d say AGI by 2036 gives working musicians time to strengthen the teaching side and save. Ten years of warning is no contract for next month’s café set.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could build reliable lessons and maybe share the community room with another teacher. I am not sure parents will pay for ten years, so I would keep the plan small and check each term.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting next term I’d ask for standing bookings from the three pupil families and set aside fifteen from each paid café set. In the first year after 2036, I’d use the community room only if those lessons still cover its rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m uneasy about the future, and anxious about the next rent payment. Ten years gives me time to save, but it does not pay this month’s bill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much would you hope to save?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First I want one month of bills saved, then three. I would count only money already in the account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who could share the room?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The guitar teacher downstairs might want to share the room. I would ask about her schedule and costs before signing anything.

say: I’d tell musicians to strengthen **teaching** and save during the decade before 2036.
I would still get **café dates** in writing, because ten years of warning is no contract.
think: Reliable **lesson bookings** might let me share a room without taking on a large new cost.
I cannot assume **parents** will pay for a decade, so I need to check every term.
do: Ask the three pupil families for **standing bookings** next term.
Set aside **fifteen** from each paid café set and rent community space only if lessons cover it after 2036.
feel: I feel **anxious** about this month’s rent, even with more time to prepare for later change.
fieldNote: A long horizon softens the AI threat but does not erase his current **cash shortage**.
He will not sign a **shared-room** lease until he checks schedules and whether lessons cover rent.
S4.quote: Ten years of warning is no contract for next month’s café set.

steps.text: Ask three pupil families for standing lesson bookings next term
Save fifteen from each paid café set

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most, because arranging could dry up before I have savings or a full teaching week. A cheap community room and clear, paid bookings would help me keep work together.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You might ask why I still practise for an hour when the café pays so little. Practising is how I keep a promise to the people who come to hear me, even when the fee barely covers the week.

headlineQuote: Practising is how I keep a promise to the people who come to hear me, even when the fee barely covers the week.
portrait: At **27**, Adam plays piano, arranges scores and teaches after earning a music master’s degree.
His high **skill** brings trust, but low and irregular pay leaves less than one month of savings.
He uses AI **occasionally** and wants an experienced musician to show him where generated scores fail.
Fast **2028 AGI** threatens arrangements first; he tests group teaching before signing costly space.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove arranging fees before he has savings or enough teaching hours.
whatWouldHelp: Affordable **community space** and firm paid bookings would help him keep lessons going.
